newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian currencies quiet but Taiwan dollar battered
newsitem.headline: Asian currencies quiet but Taiwan dollar battered

text.p: The Taiwan dollar stood out among otherwise quiet Asia regional currencies on Wednesay, with a further plunge to its lowest level in nine years against the U.S. dollar.

The Taiwan dollar has been hammered since the central bank dropped its defence of the T$28 level on Tuesday. It was the first time since 1989 the authorities had allowed the currency to fall below that level.

But given the recent falls in currencies around the region, the central bank's decision made perfect sense economically and while the timing may have been somewhat of a surprise, the move itself was not, analsyts said.

"The Southeast Asian countries which have devalued account for about 10 percent of Taiwan's export market and also they are competitors of Taiwan in third markets as well," said Chi Lo, regional economist, North-East Asia at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Singapore.
"If you have your competitors devaluing, in some cases more than 15 percent, there is tremendous amount of pressure to follow."
He said that for the 18 months, the Taiwan dollar had been lagging in terms of depreciating against the U.S. dollar, leaving Taiwan at a competitive disadvantage on the trade front.
Analysts and dealers are looking at T$29 and reckon the central bank will be happy for a decline to that level providing the decline does not turn into a free fall.
The central bank vowed again on Wednesday to remain "hands-off" in the forex market, but dealers suspect it will step in to calm things down should the fall become precipitous.
At 0900 GMT the Taiwan dollar was trading at 28.455/489 per U.S. dollar compared with Tuesday's finish of 28.170.
Elsewhere among Asian regional currencies things were pretty slack with traders unwilling to take fresh positions ahead of the month end.
There was still the problem of the firm U.S. dollar with importers picking up cheap dollars each time it fell and nervous exporters were still looking to hedge more of their portfolio positions.

While optimism about Thailand's plans to seek assistance from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in rehabilitating its troubled economy continued to underpin regional currencies generally, the baht gave futher ground.
The onshore rate edged down to a late 31.900/32.200 against 31.500/31.800 late on Tuesday. It was trading at 31.600/31.800 offshore.
In Malaysia, Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's continued tirade against currency speculation spurred further caution as the Malaysian premier extended his criticism to local operators.
"The market feels that if he continues to talk this way, there may be some action down the line. So people are wary," said an analyst with a research firm in Singapore.
Dealers said Mahathir's remarks were prompting Kuala Lumpur corporates and exporters to sell the dollar on any rallies.
The ringgit was at 2.6265/75 to the dollar, down on levels seen late on Tuesday around 2.6150.
The Singapore dollar edged lower to a late 1.1.4670/80 from 1.4620 on Tuesady.

The Indonesian rupiah remained ensconced above the 2,600 level, but dealers said local operators continued to buy dollars following central bank statements that a normal level for the rupiah was between 2,555 and 2,610.
Spot rupiah was quoted at 2,580/90 in late business, little changed from Tuesday's close.
Indonesia's central bank was reported to have sold $1 billion in the forward market to stabilise the rupiah during last week's speculative attack.

The Philippine central bank sold dollars at the higher level of 29 pesos amid persistent dollar demand from commercial clients. Traders said the demand was unlikely to subside and the peso would fall sharply if the central bank did not step in.
